    Cleaning: From Raw Records to Tidy Text

    Last updated on 2026-11-11 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What do raw bibliographic records look like, and how do we get to know an unfamiliar export?
    • What is “formal noise” in catalogue data, and how do we remove it?
    • How does the fennica R package clean bibliographic records, and how can we reuse its approach?

    Objectives

    • Profile a raw dataset: unique values, missing values and the most common forms.
    • Clean text fields with regular expressions (grepl(), gsub(), sub()).
    • Recognise the different ways in which a catalogue says “unknown”.
    • Clean personal names with polish_author() from the fennica package, and check its result on difficult names.
    • Write each cleaning step as a function, and apply it to unique values only.
    • Read a cleaning function from the fennica package and judge which parts fit another bibliography.

    Making the data ready for analysis

    Throughout this course we follow one research question:

    How did the shift from Swedish to Finnish in publishing happen in 19th-century Finland, and how certain can we be about it?

    To study it we need, for every publication, at least its language, its place of publication, its publisher and its author. None of these exists as a clean variable in the library catalogue. The next four episodes make the data ready for analysis, in four steps:

    Step Question Episode
    Cleaning Is the text free of formal noise? this episode
    Harmonisation Does one thing have one name? Harmonisation
    Enrichment What can other sources add? Enrichment
    Validation How far can we trust the result? Validation

    In this episode we only clean: we remove what is not part of the data (cataloguing punctuation, brackets, extra spaces) and turn the many ways of saying “unknown” into missing values. We do not yet decide that Helsingfors and Helsinki are the same town; that is harmonisation.

    Callout

    Data has a history

    A catalogue record is not the book itself but a description of it, made by a cataloguer, often a century or more after printing, following cataloguing rules that have changed over time. The record was then edited, digitised, exported and processed. Each step can add variation (many spellings of the same name), missing values (unknown publisher) or errors. Keep asking: what process produced this value? The answer decides how we clean it, and later, how certain our conclusions can be.

    The fennica package

    The Fennica data has already been cleaned and harmonised once, with the R package fennica. It has one polish_*() function per field, for example polish_publisher(), polish_place(), polish_author() and polish_languages(), and a set of lookup tables in the folder inst/extdata.

    We do not install the package. Instead, we build simplified versions of its functions step by step, so that we understand every decision, and we read the real functions to see how the project solved the same problems. This is also how you would adapt the package to another bibliography.

    A first look at the raw records

    The file priority_fields19.feather contains the raw catalogue records of all Fennica publications from 1809 to 1917, exported from the National Library of Finland’s catalogue. Only the most important (priority) MARC fields are included.

    R 

    raw <- read_ipc_file("data/priority_fields19.feather")
dim(raw)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 72626    60

    R 

    names(raw)

    OUTPUT 

     [1] "id"                    "fikka_id"              "leader"
 [4] "field_008"             "other_system_id"       "author_name"
 [7] "author_date"           "language_work"         "asteri_id"
[10] "language_041"          "language_original"     "title_uniform"
[13] "title"                 "title_remainder"       "title_part_number"
[16] "publication_place"     "publisher"             "publication_place_264"
[19] "physical_dimensions"   "physical_extent"       "publication_frequency"
[22] "publication_dates"     "UDC"                   "UDC_aux"
[25] "classification_084"    "genre_655"             "genre_655_source"
[28] "subject_650"           "note_500"              "content_type_336"
[31] "contents_505"          "summary_520"           "variant_title_246"
[34] "title_uniform_130"     "title2"                "type_of_record"
[37] "bibliographic_level"   "Date_entered"          "publication_status"
[40] "publication_time"      "field_008_33"          "data_element_008"
[43] "converted_008_33"      "language_008"          "location_a"
[46] "institution_code"      "sublocation"           "shelving_location"
[49] "address"               "coded_location"        "noncoded_location"
[52] "url"                   "call_number"           "item_part"
[55] "shelving_control"      "call_number_prefix"    "call_number_suffix"
[58] "piece_designation"     "nonpublic_note"        "public_note"

    The columns have readable names, but each one comes from a MARC field: a three-digit field number and a subfield letter. The ones we use are:

    Column MARC field Content
    id 001 record identifier
    field_008 008 fixed-length coded data (dates, language, …)
    author_name 100a main author: name
    author_date 100d main author: years of life
    asteri_id 100 (authority link) main author: identifier in the authority file
    language_041 041a language code(s)
    language_008 008/35–37 language code inside field 008
    publication_place 260a place of publication
    publisher 260b publisher
    publication_place_264 264a place of publication (newer rules)
    physical_extent 300a number of pages, or type of resource

    We keep only these columns, with short names:

    R 

    records <- raw |>
  select(id, field_008,
         author = author_name, author_date, asteri_id,
         language_041, language_008,
         place_260 = publication_place, place_264 = publication_place_264,
         publisher, extent = physical_extent)

    Profiling: how messy is each column?

    Before cleaning anything we want an overview: how many different values does each column have, and how much is missing? We write a function for it, because we will use it again and again:

    R 

    is_blank <- function(x) is.na(x) | str_trim(x) == ""

profile <- function(data) {
  data |>
    summarise(across(everything(), list(
      n_unique = \(x) n_distinct(x[!is_blank(x)]),
      pct_missing = \(x) round(100 * mean(is_blank(x)), 1)
    ))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(),
                 names_to = c("column", ".value"),
                 names_pattern = "(.*)_(n_unique|pct_missing)")
}

profile(records)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 11 × 3
   column       n_unique pct_missing
   <chr>           <int>       <dbl>
 1 id              72626         0
 2 field_008       51019         0
 3 author          11103        37.5
 4 author_date      3758        56.7
 5 asteri_id        4692        52.4
 6 language_041      241         1.8
 7 language_008       42         0.8
 8 place_260        1299        28.7
 9 place_264        1272        73.2
10 publisher        9889        29.3
11 extent          17080         9.1

    across() applies the two summaries to every column, and pivot_longer() turns the one-row result into one row per column. (\(x) is a short way of writing function(x).) We will also often need the number of unique, non-missing values of a single column:

    R 

    n_unique <- function(x) n_distinct(x[!is_blank(x)])
n_unique(records$place_260)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 1299

    A few numbers stand out already:

    • 1,299 different places of publication, although Finland had only a few dozen printing towns;
    • 9,889 different publishers;
    • 241 different “languages”;
    • about a third of the records have no author, and almost a third have no place in field 260.

    Regular expressions: a quick reference

    We clean text with regular expressions (regex), small patterns that describe text:

    • grepl(pattern, x): does each value contain the pattern? (TRUE/FALSE)
    • sub(pattern, replacement, x): replace the first match; gsub() replaces all matches.
    Pattern Meaning Example Matches
    ^ / $ start / end of the text ^Hels “Helsinki”
    . any character H.lsinki “Helsinki”, “Hälsinki”
    [abc] one of these characters [,.:] a comma, full stop or colon
    \\s a space \\s*: “:”, ” :“,” :”
    + / * one or more / zero or more [,.]+$ “,”, “.,” at the end
    a\|b a or b Turku\|Åbo “Turku” or “Åbo”
    ( ) and \\1 capture a group, and reuse it ^([0-9]{4})-.* “1818-1898” → “1818”
    \\b word boundary \\bförf\\b “förf”, not “förfat”

    Characters such as [ ] . | ( ) have special meanings; to match them literally, escape them (\\[, \\.) or put them inside brackets ([|]).

    R 

    places <- c("Helsinki :", "[Helsinki] :", "Turku,", "Helsingfors :")
gsub("\\s*[:,]$", "", places)   # remove a final colon or comma

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Helsinki"    "[Helsinki]"  "Turku"       "Helsingfors"

    R 

    gsub("\\[|\\]", "", places)     # remove square brackets

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Helsinki :"    "Helsinki :"    "Turku,"        "Helsingfors :"

    Formal noise: punctuation and brackets

    R 

    records |> count(place_260, sort = TRUE) |> head(15)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 15 × 2
   place_260                          n
   <chr>                          <int>
 1 <NA>                           20812
 2 Helsinki :                     13566
 3 Helsingfors :                  11025
 4 Porvoo :                        2580
 5 Tampere :                       2176
 6 Kuopio :                        1417
 7 Turku :                         1367
 8 Hämeenlinna :                   1113
 9 [Kustannuspaikka tuntematon] :  1067
10 Jyväskylä :                      924
11 Stockholm :                      917
12 Åbo :                            875
13 [S.l.] :                         692
14 Aboae :                          619
15 Pori :                           616

    Two kinds of problems are mixed here. Some are formal noise, which is not part of the data:

    • cataloguing punctuation (Helsinki :): it separates MARC subfields;
    • square brackets ([Helsinki] :): the place is not printed in the book but was added by the cataloguer;
    • extra spaces and differences in upper and lower case.

    Others are real variation in the names: Helsingfors is the Swedish name of Helsinki, and Helsingissä means “in Helsinki”. We leave those for the next episode. A cleaning function removes only the formal noise:

    R 

    clean_place_text <- function(x) {
  x <- sub("[|].*", "", x)                 # keep the first place
  x <- gsub("\\[|\\]|\"", "", x)           # brackets and quotes
  x <- gsub("\\s*[:;,.]+\\s*$", "", x)     # final punctuation
  x <- str_squish(x)                       # extra spaces
  tolower(x)
}

place_text <- clean_place_text(records$place_260)
n_unique(records$place_260)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 1299

    R 

    n_unique(place_text)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 897

    Cleaning alone removes a large part of the apparent variation.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Brackets carry information

    Square brackets mean that the cataloguer added the place: it is not printed in the book. What share of the non-missing places in field 260 are in brackets? Our clean_place_text() removes the brackets. What do we lose, and how could we keep that information?

    R 

    has_place <- !is_blank(records$place_260)
mean(grepl("^\\[", records$place_260[has_place]))

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 0.06598603

    About 7% of the places were added by a cataloguer. They are usually right, but they are an inference, not a fact printed in the book. Removing the brackets silently throws that difference away. A good solution is to keep it in a separate variable before cleaning:

    R 

    place_inferred <- grepl("^\\[", records$place_260)

    Cleaning should never remove information we may need later; if in doubt, store it in a new column.

    Many ways to say “unknown”

    A catalogue rarely leaves a field empty when the information is unknown. It writes a phrase instead:

    R 

    tibble(place = place_text) |>
  filter(grepl("tuntematon|^s\\.? ?l$", place)) |>
  count(place, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(6)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 6 × 2
  place                                                                        n
  <chr>                                                                    <int>
1 kustannuspaikka tuntematon                                                1103
2 kustantaja tuntematon                                                        7
3 s.l                                                                          4
4 helsinki kustantaja tuntematon                                               2
5 kristinestad? : kustantaja tuntematon                                        2
6 kustannuspaikka tuntematon : ohion, pennsylvanian ja west virginian suo…     2

    Kustannuspaikka tuntematon is Finnish for “place of publication unknown”, kustantaja tuntematon for “publisher unknown”, and s.l. (sine loco) and s.n. (sine nomine) are the Latin equivalents. For statistics, they are all missing values, and they must become NA. Otherwise “kustannuspaikka tuntematon” would appear as one of the largest publishing places in Finland!

    R 

    is_unknown <- function(x) {
  grepl("^(kustannuspaikka|kustantaja) tuntematon$|^s\\.? ?[ln]$", x)
}

place_text[is_unknown(place_text)] <- NA
sum(is.na(place_text))

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 21928
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Why ^ and $?

    The pattern in is_unknown() starts with ^ and ends with $, so it only matches values that are nothing but an unknown phrase. Find the values of clean_place_text(records$place_260) that contain “tuntematon” but are not caught by is_unknown(). What would have happened if we had simply used grepl("tuntematon", x)?

    R 

    all_places <- clean_place_text(records$place_260)
all_places[grepl("tuntematon", all_places) & !is_unknown(all_places)] |>
  table() |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  head(5)

    OUTPUT 

    
                                                                helsinki kustantaja tuntematon
                                                                                             2
                                                             käkisalmi : kustantaja tuntematon
                                                                                             2
                                                         kristinestad? : kustantaja tuntematon
                                                                                             2
kustannuspaikka tuntematon : ohion, pennsylvanian ja west virginian suomalainen raittiusliitto
                                                                                             2
                                                                  ekenäs kustantaja tuntematon
                                                                                             1

    In these records the place and the publisher ended up in the same subfield: “helsinki kustantaja tuntematon” means “Helsinki, publisher unknown”. The place is known! A pattern without ^ and $ would have deleted it. Anchoring makes a rule stricter, and a strict rule is easier to trust.

    Publisher

    The same cleaning works for the publisher. One extra rule removes the word distr. or jakaja (“distributor”):

    R 

    clean_publisher_text <- function(x) {
  x <- clean_place_text(x)
  gsub(",? *(i )?(distr\\.?|jakaja)$", "", x)
}

publisher_text <- clean_publisher_text(records$publisher)
n_unique(records$publisher)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 9889

    R 

    n_unique(publisher_text)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 8305

    The real polish_publisher() contains dozens of rules like ours, for example:

    R 

    x <- gsub("\\bförfattaren\\b|\\bförfattare\\b|\\bförf\\b|\\btekijät\\b",
          "tekijä", x, perl = TRUE)
x <- gsub("\\bsöderstörm\\b", "söderström", x, perl = TRUE)  # a typo

    \\b is a word boundary: it makes sure that \\bförf\\b matches the abbreviation förf, but not the start of a longer word:

    R 

    words <- c("förf", "förf.", "förfat", "en förf")
grepl("förf", words)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE

    R 

    grepl("\\bförf\\b", words)

    OUTPUT 

    [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

    Author names

    The main author is in MARC field 100, subfield $a, written in inverted form: surname, first names. Let’s look at the most common values:

    R 

    records |> count(author, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 8 × 2
  author                            n
  <chr>                         <int>
1 <NA>                          27270
2 Topelius, Zacharias,            711
3 Runeberg, Johan Ludvig,         483
4 Sjöström, Axel Gabriel,         326
5 Luther, Martti,                 259
6 Aho, Juhani,                    207
7 Rein, Gabriel,                  153
8 Sahlberg, Carolus Reginaldus,   138

    Cataloguing punctuation

    Every name ends with cataloguing punctuation, and not always the same one:

    R 

    table(str_sub(records$author, -1)) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(4)

    OUTPUT 

    
    ,     .     n     i
33406 11893    10     8

    Most names end with a comma (field 100 continues with the years of life in subfield $d), others with a full stop. As a result, the same person appears several times:

    R 

    records |>
  filter(grepl("^Benedix, Julius", author)) |>
  count(author)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 3 × 2
  author                         n
  <chr>                      <int>
1 Benedix, Julius Roderich,      1
2 Benedix, Julius Roderich.     12
3 Benedix, Julius Roderich.,     1

    Brackets and parentheses

    A few names contain a second form of the name in brackets or parentheses:

    R 

    records |>
  filter(grepl("[][()]", author)) |>
  count(author)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 8 × 2
  author                                        n
  <chr>                                     <int>
1 A[sup ***].                                   1
2 Heikel, Fredrik Hjalmar (Jalmari).            1
3 Krüger, Stephanus Johannes Paulus (Paul).     1
4 Ridge, John James [Jaakko].                   1
5 Siltala (Silfvenius), A. J.                   1
6 Stenwall, Hanna [Kiwi].                       1
7 Tollstadius, Erik [Eerikki].                  1
8 [Engelberg, G.].                              1

    Look at them carefully. Stenwall, Hanna [Kiwi], Tollstadius, Erik [Eerikki] and Heikel, Fredrik Hjalmar (Jalmari) add the Finnish form of a Swedish name: these authors used both. That is exactly the kind of detail our running question is about, so we keep it in its own column before we remove it from the name. str_match() returns the part of the text inside the parentheses ( ) of the pattern:

    R 

    other_name <- str_match(records$author, "\\s[\\[(]([^])]*)[])]")[, 2]
table(other_name)

    OUTPUT 

    other_name
   Eerikki     Jaakko    Jalmari       Kiwi       Paul Silfvenius
         1          1          1          1          1          1

    One name is different: in [Engelberg, G.] the whole name is in brackets. As with places, this means the name is not printed in the book: the cataloguer identified the author. Here we remove only the brackets.

    Transliterated names

    Names from Russian are transliterated from the Cyrillic alphabet:

    R 

    records |>
  filter(grepl("\"", author)) |>
  count(author)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 6 × 2
  author                              n
  <chr>                           <int>
1 "Buslaev\", F̀. I."                  1
2 "Fedorov\", F. A."                  1
3 "Gogol', Nikolaj Vasil'evič\"."     1
4 "Granstrem\", È,"                   2
5 "Kaulbars\", N."                    1
6 "Kaulbars\", Nikolai,"              1

    The " after Fedorov or Kaulbars stands for the Russian “hard sign” (ъ), which the old Russian spelling wrote at the end of many words. It is not part of the name in Finnish or Swedish texts, so we remove it.

    The fennica function: polish_author()

    The fennica package has a function for exactly this job: polish_author(). We do not need to install the whole package to use it. An R function is just code, and source() can run code directly from GitHub. polish_author() uses five small helper functions from the package, so we load those too:

    R 

    fennica_code <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fennicahub/fennica/",
                       "e1c7bbd7337b84d3acc9d890ed843a80b0f14fba/R/")

for (f in c("polish_author", "pick_firstname", "pick_lastname",
            "capitalize", "condense_spaces", "clean_name_col")) {
  source(paste0(fennica_code, f, ".R"))
}

    The long code in the address is a commit: one fixed version of the package. If the package changes later, our results stay the same. This is an important habit for reproducible research: always know which version of someone else’s code you used. (polish_author() also needs the package stringi; install it with install.packages("stringi") if you don’t have it.)

    Let’s try it on the names we have seen:

    R 

    examples <- c("Benedix, Julius Roderich.,", "Runeberg, Johan Ludvig,",
              "Setälä, E. N.,", "Kaulbars\", Nikolai,",
              "Stenwall, Hanna [Kiwi].")
polish_author(examples)

    OUTPUT 

                     full_name           first      last
1 Benedix, Julius Roderich Julius Roderich   Benedix
2   Runeberg, Johan Ludvig    Johan Ludvig  Runeberg
3              Setälä, E N             E N    Setälä
4       Kaulbars", Nikolai         Nikolai Kaulbars"
5   Stenwall, Hanna [kiwi]    Hanna [kiwi]  Stenwall

    polish_author() returns a data frame with three columns: the full name and, separately, the last and first names. Reading its code on GitHub, we can see the steps:

    1. convert to lower case, and work on unique values only;
    2. remove final commas, digits and (meant to remove) brackets;
    3. split the name into last and first name: at the comma if there is one, otherwise at the last space;
    4. capitalise each word, and replace full stops with spaces (E. N. → E N);
    5. glue the parts together again as last, first.

    Now on all records:

    R 

    polished <- polish_author(records$author)
n_unique(records$author)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 11103

    R 

    n_unique(polished$full_name)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 10475

    Checking what the function did

    A ready-made function is a set of decisions made by someone else, for their data. Before we trust it, we look at what it does to our data. Some harder cases:

    R 

    harder <- c("Thomas Ragvaldinpoika,", "K. H. T.", "Larin-Kyösti,",
            "Åkerman, Anna", "Daniel Henkikäsi, numero 3.",
            "Lindroth, Hjalmar,|1878-1947,")
tibble(raw = harder, polished = polish_author(harder)$full_name)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 6 × 2
  raw                           polished
  <chr>                         <chr>
1 Thomas Ragvaldinpoika,        Ragvaldinpoika, Thomas
2 K. H. T.                      T, K
3 Larin-Kyösti,                 Larin-kyösti
4 Åkerman, Anna                 åkerman, Anna
5 Daniel Henkikäsi, numero 3.   Daniel Henkikäsi, Numero
6 Lindroth, Hjalmar,|1878-1947, Lindroth, Hjalmar,|-

    Each line shows a decision that does not fit every name:

    • Thomas Ragvaldinpoika is a patronymic (“son of Ragvald”), an older Nordic naming practice: there is no surname. The rule “the last word is the surname” turns it into Ragvaldinpoika, Thomas.
    • K. H. T. is a signature, not a name, and is split as if it were one.
    • Larin-Kyösti is a pseudonym; capitalising “each word” lower-cases the part after the hyphen.
    • Åkerman stays in lower case: the capitalisation only knows the letters a–z, not å, ä and ö.
    • Removing all digits changes numero 3 (part of a pseudonym) and leaves a dash behind from the years of life in Lindroth.
    • The brackets in Stenwall, Hanna [Kiwi] above were not removed: inside [ ], R’s regular expressions do not treat \\ as an escape character, so the pattern in the function does not match brackets. The pattern "[][()?]" would.

    None of this makes the function useless: for the large majority of names it does exactly the right thing. But it shows what a cleaning function really is: rules that fit most of the data. Our job is to find the cases they don’t fit, and to decide whether to change the rules, add exceptions, or flag the records.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Names that start in lower case

    After polish_author(), a name should start with a capital letter. Count the polished names that start with a lower-case letter. Which letters are they? How would you fix the problem: in the function, or after it?

    R 

    polished |>
  filter(grepl("^[[:lower:]]", full_name)) |>
  count(first_letter = str_sub(full_name, 1, 1), sort = TRUE)

    OUTPUT 

      first_letter   n
1            å 139
2            ö 128
3            ä  18
4            š   8
5            á   1
6            ż   1

    R 

    polished |>
  filter(grepl("^[[:lower:]]", full_name)) |>
  count(full_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)

    OUTPUT 

              full_name  n
1 öhquist, Johannes 33
2 åberg, Johan Olof 31
3         åström, N 24
4        åberg, J O 21
5  åkerblom, Rudolf 12

    Almost all of them are Swedish and Finnish names starting with Å, Ö or Ä, plus a few names with letters from other alphabets (š, á, ż). The clean fix is in the function: capitalize() loops over letters, the 26 letters of the English alphabet. Using toupper() on the first character, which knows all letters, fixes it for every language. Fixing it in the function helps everyone who uses the package; fixing it after the function only helps us. This is how open-source tools improve: users find a case that does not fit, and report or fix it.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Names that are not names

    An author name in field 100 normally has the form surname, first names. Find the raw author names (after removing the final punctuation) that contain no comma. What are they? What does polish_author() do with them, and what should be done with them?

    R 

    no_comma <- records |>
  mutate(author = str_squish(gsub("[,.]+$", "", author))) |>
  filter(!is_blank(author), !grepl(",", author)) |>
  count(author, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)

no_comma |>
  mutate(polished = polish_author(author)$full_name)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 8 × 3
  author                         n polished
  <chr>                      <int> <chr>
1 Larin-Kyösti                  80 Larin-kyösti
2 Aina                          79 Aina
3 Thomas Ragvaldinpoika         78 Ragvaldinpoika, Thomas
4 Maria                         71 Maria
5 Kauppis-Heikki                35 Kauppis-heikki
6 Parus Ater                    25 Ater, Parus
7 Catharina Johanneksentytär    20 Johanneksentytär, Catharina
8 Suonio                        19 Suonio

    Several different things are hidden here:

    • pseudonyms: Larin-Kyösti (Karl Gustaf Larson), Suonio (Julius Krohn), Kauppis-Heikki (Heikki Kauppinen), and Parus Ater (Latin for “coal tit”), which polish_author() turns into Ater, Parus;
    • patronymics without a surname: Thomas Ragvaldinpoika (“son of Ragvald”), Catharina Johanneksentytär (“daughter of Johannes”);
    • single first names, such as Aina and Maria, and initials with which authors signed their books.

    Patronymics are real names and should be kept as they are: reversing them into “surname, first name” is wrong. Pseudonyms and initials cannot be turned into persons with a regular expression. We can only flag these records, for example with a variable author_no_surname, and leave the identification to authority data and research. Other differences, such as Setälä, E. N. and Setälä, Emil Nestor, are not formal noise either: merging them is harmonisation, the topic of the next episode.

    A second, simpler version

    The Fennica project’s harmonised data already contains the output of polish_author(). To be able to check it in the episode on validation, we also write a deliberately simple cleaning function of our own. It removes only formal noise, and keeps the name order as the cataloguer wrote it:

    R 

    clean_author <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("\"", "", x)                       # transliterated hard sign
  x <- gsub("\\s+[\\[(][^])]*[])]", "", x)     # other forms: [Kiwi], (Jalmari)
  x <- gsub("^\\[(.*)\\][.,]*$", "\\1", x)     # whole name added by the cataloguer
  x <- gsub("[,.]+$", "", x)                   # final punctuation
  str_squish(x)                                # extra spaces
}

clean_author(c("Benedix, Julius Roderich.,", "Stenwall, Hanna [Kiwi].",
               "[Engelberg, G.].", "Thomas Ragvaldinpoika,"))

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Benedix, Julius Roderich" "Stenwall, Hanna"
[3] "Engelberg, G"             "Thomas Ragvaldinpoika"

    R 

    author <- clean_author(records$author)
n_unique(author)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 10507

    The order of the steps matters: the inner brackets go first, so that a name entirely in brackets is not deleted. Two independent versions of the same variable are a powerful check: wherever they disagree, at least one of them is wrong.

    Applying a function to unique values only

    Our cleaning functions look at every record, but there are only 9,889 different publisher values for 72,626 records. The fennica functions therefore clean each unique value once and map the result back to all records with match(). We can write this pattern as a general helper:

    R 

    map_unique <- function(x, f, ...) {
  values <- unique(x)
  f(values, ...)[match(x, values)]
}

publisher_text <- map_unique(records$publisher, clean_publisher_text)

    The result is identical, but for slow functions (and millions of records) the difference in speed is enormous.

    Challenge

    Challenge 5: Reuse or rewrite?

    Open polish_publisher() on GitHub. Find two rules that would work for any bibliography, and two that only make sense for Fennica. What would you change to use the function on the national bibliography of another country?

    There is no single right answer. Rules that remove punctuation, brackets and extra spaces are general. Rules that recognise Finnish and Swedish words (tekijä, förf, tuntematon), fix typos in specific publisher names, or merge the names of Finnish publishing houses are specific to Fennica. To reuse the function, keep the general steps, move the language- and country-specific words into a lookup table, and replace that table for the new bibliography.

    Callout

    Keep the cleaning in a script

    Save the cleaning functions in one script and run it from the raw data every time. Never edit the raw data by hand. Our version is here: clean_records.R. The next episode starts from it.

    Key Points
    • Start with a profile of the data: unique values, missing values and the most common forms.
    • Cleaning removes formal noise (punctuation, brackets, spaces); harmonisation, in the next episode, merges real variants.
    • Catalogues have many ways of saying “unknown”; turn them into NA, with strict, anchored patterns.
    • Cleaning should not destroy information: keep things like “added by the cataloguer” or an alternative name form in a separate column.
    • A ready-made function such as polish_author() is a set of rules that fit most of the data: check what it does to yours, and load a fixed version (commit) of it.
    • Some values, such as patronymics, initials and pseudonyms, do not fit the rules; keep or flag them instead.
    • Write each cleaning step as a function, and apply slow functions to unique values only.
    • The fennica package can be reused, but its language- and country-specific rules must be adapted.
